function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

**Java** is a high‑level, class‑based, object‑oriented programming language that was first released by Sun Microsystems in 1995 (now owned by Oracle). It’s designed to be:

| Feature | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Write once, run anywhere (WORA)** | Java programs compile to bytecode that runs on any device with a Java Virtual Machine (JVM). |
| **Object‑oriented** | Everything is an object (except primitives), encouraging modular, reusable code. |
| **Strongly typed** | Types are checked at compile time, reducing runtime errors. |
| **Platform‑independent** | The same `.class` files run on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, etc. |
| **Robust & secure** | Built‑in exception handling, garbage collection, and a sandboxed execution environment. |

### Typical uses

| Domain | Why Java fits |
|--------|---------------|
| **Enterprise applications** | Mature frameworks (Spring, Jakarta EE) and a huge ecosystem of libraries. |
| **Android apps** | Android’s SDK is built on Java (or Kotlin, which interoperates with Java). |
| **Web servers & microservices** | High performance, scalability, and mature tooling (Maven, Gradle). |
| **Big data & analytics** | Hadoop, Spark, and other big‑data tools are Java‑based. |
| **Embedded systems** | Lightweight JVMs (e.g., MicroEJ) allow Java on IoT devices. |

### Quick history

| Year | Milestone |
|------|-----------|
| 1991 | James Gosling starts “Green Project” at Sun. |
| 1995 | Java 1.0 released – “Java is fun!” |
| 1998 | Java 2 (J2SE) introduces Swing, JDBC, etc. |
| 2004 | Java 5 adds generics, annotations, enhanced for‑loop. |
| 2011 | Java 7 introduces try‑with‑resources, diamond operator. |
| 2014 | Java 8 brings lambda expressions, streams, and the new Date/Time API. |
| 2017 | Java 9 modular system (Project Jigsaw). |
| 2020 | Java 17 becomes a long‑term support (LTS) release. |

### Common misconceptions

| Myth | Reality |
|------|---------|
| **Java = JavaScript** | Completely unrelated languages; JavaScript is a scripting language for browsers. |
| **Java is slow** | Modern JVMs use just‑in‑time (JIT) compilation and advanced optimizations; Java can rival native C/C++ in many cases. |
| **Java is only for desktop** | It’s everywhere: web, mobile, cloud, embedded, and even AI frameworks. |

### Getting started

```bash
# Compile
javac HelloWorld.java

# Run
java HelloWorld
```

```java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, Java!");
    }
}
```

That’s the gist: Java is a versatile, mature language that powers a huge portion of today’s software stack.
